subject: sg-succession
note:
SIXTY-TWO FORKS ACROSS FOUR ACTS, one entry for each row of the four Act modules' own AMBIGUITY REGISTERS, which are the source of truth: wills-act.l4 A1-A11 (11), intestate-succession-act.l4 A1-A21 (21), probate-administration-act.l4 A1-A12 (12), and guardianship-of-infants-act.l4, whose register is unnumbered prose and runs 1-17 with a 4a (18). The entry ids preserve that mapping (F-WA-A1, F-ISA-A7, F-PAA-A12, F-GIA-04A) so any row of this file can be read against the comment that produced it, and the comment against the source text.

COMPLETENESS IS NOT CLAIMED AND CANNOT BE. No procedure establishes that every ambiguity in four Acts has been found. What this register does claim is narrower and checkable: every numbered row of every module's own register is here, and every quoted phrase is verbatim from source/*.txt in this directory. Where the modules recorded a SUB-fork inside a numbered row -- there are five, at GIA entries 3, 4a, 5, 10 and 13 -- it is carried in that entry's `notes` rather than promoted to an entry of its own, so the 1:1 map with the module registers survives.

NO ENTRY IS MATERIALISED AS AN `interpretation-field`, AND THAT IS A FACT ABOUT THE CODE RATHER THAN A CHOICE HERE. R4's shape is a field of an `Interpretation` record threaded as an ordinary GIVEN; no such record exists anywhere in this cleanroom -- `grep -n Interpretation *.l4` over this directory returns five lines -- the four Acts' own interpretation-section headings and one prose reference to the Wills Act's -- and no `DECLARE` of a record by that or any equivalent name. `interpretation_type` is therefore omitted rather than asserted. Fifty-seven entries are `resolved-at-encode` and five are `delegated-to-fact` -- F-ISA-A1 (who is a Muslim), F-PAA-A4 (whose minority), F-GIA-01 (the age of an infant), F-GIA-09 (whether income is insufficient) and F-GIA-12 (the unit of access). Fifty-nine entries are `resolved` and three are `open`: F-ISA-A4, where both readings are encoded side by side and neither drives the answer alone, and F-GIA-01 and F-GIA-11, where the module's own register says in terms 'TAKEN: neither'. The schema requires a `taken` even on an `open` entry, so in those three it records what the encoding does rather than a choice between the readings, and each says so at the site.

NO ENTRY IS `settled`, AND THAT IS THE HONEST READING OF THE P2 SWEEP. external-modifications.json holds forty-six entries -- twelve binding, twenty-eight interpretive, six prospective -- and not one of them settles a fork in this register: the age of an infant under the Guardianship of Infants Act is stated at 21 by a rule of court (E1), by an obiter parenthesis (E2) and by a public web page (E3), none of which is that Act; VET v VEU (E38, E39) and UPD v UPC (E44) construe who is a guardian and pull in opposite directions; Cheng Tze Tzuen and Toh Seok Kheng (E19) supply a priority for a grant without deciding who the next of kin ARE, which is the fork PAA A3 states. Twenty-one entries carry a `cross_refs` link to a P2 entry that bears on them; the rest carry the empty array, which says nothing bears on them and not that nobody looked.

DIVERGENCE IS CLAIMED ONLY WHERE A NAMED FIXTURE SEPARATES THE READINGS. intestate-succession-act.l4 keeps its own index of which case exhibits which ambiguity (at `Worked cases -- what the rules actually produce`), and this register follows it rather than re-deriving it; the one place it goes beyond that index is F-ISA-A11, where cases 7 and 7a plainly separate priority from concurrent abatement and the module's index omits the row. Elsewhere `unassessed` means what it says -- honest at P4 time, and what forbids a later report from claiming an interpretation-independence nobody measured.

THIS FILE SUPERSEDES jl4/examples/legal/sg-succession/denovo/fork-register.json, WHICH IS NOT AN EARLIER VERSION OF IT. That register has seven entries over THREE of these Acts and describes a DIFFERENT ENCODING (jl4/examples/legal/sg-succession/sg-isa.l4, sg-paa.l4, sg-succession-domain.l4), written independently. The two are not versions of each other and must not be diffed as though they were: where they agree -- the half-blood priority in ISA s 6(b), which is denovo F6 and F-ISA-A11 here -- two encodings reached the same reading by different routes, and where they differ the difference may be the encoding and not the law. denovo's file is left on disk as the record of what was deposited then.

site.anchor: `the age of the testator when the will was made`

source.quote: No will made by any person under 21 years of age shall be valid.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 4

readings.description: s 4 is a DISQUALIFICATION. The will stands unless infancy at execution is proved, so an unproved age leaves the will valid so far as s 4 is concerned.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 4 -- the section is framed as a disability of a class of testator ('No will made by any person under 21 years of age'), and a disability must be established against the person it is asserted of

readings.foreclosure: Nothing refutes it -- it is the ordinary way a statutory disqualification is pleaded, and neither the Act nor any authority found in the P2 sweep displaces it. It is non-operative here only because the encoding refuses to report a will as NOT made by an infant when nobody knows when the testator was born; the enum's third member exists so that the case is visible rather than folded either way.

readings.description: Formal validity must be AFFIRMATIVELY ESTABLISHED, so an unproved age satisfies neither limb: the will is not shown to be an infant's, and the testator is not shown to have been 21 or over.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 6(1) -- 'No will shall be valid unless it is in writing and executed in the manner mentioned in subsection (2)'
Wills Act 1838 s 7(1) -- 'No appointment made by will, in exercise of any power, shall be valid, unless the will is executed in the manner required by this Act.'

taken.rationale: `Whether the testator had attained 21 years of age when the will was made` is a THREE-member enum, and the affirmative limb is `21 years of age or over` rather than the negation of `under 21 years of age`, so an unproved age falls into `not in evidence, the date of birth of the testator or the date of execution of the will not being known` and `the formal validity of the will` reports that s 4 could not be applied. The Act frames validity negatively throughout, which puts the burden on the propounder. NOTE THE THREE-WAY SPLIT ACROSS THE CORPUS, recorded at the site as cross-module finding X5: this Act carries a third value, probate-administration-act.l4 folds the same silence to FALSE (F-PAA-A2), and guardianship-of-infants-act.l4 propagates NOTHING (F-GIA-17). None of the three is said to be wrong; this Act differs because s 4 states its own number and names no forum for finding a testator's age, while PAA s 6(3) does name one.

witnesses: `the case of a will whose date of execution is not in evidence`

site.anchor: `falls strictly after`

source.quote: This section shall not apply to a will of a testator who died before 26 June 1992 and shall apply to a will of a testator who dies after that date whether the will was executed before or after that date.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 5(9)
Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 10(4) -- 'Subsection (3) shall apply to the will of any person dying after 29 May 1992, whether executed before or after 29 May 1992.'

readings.description: STRICTLY AFTER. A death on the named day itself falls in neither limb, so the later provision does not reach it. s 5(9) makes the gap visible: it excludes a death 'before 26 June 1992' and includes one 'after that date', and says nothing about the day.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 5(9) -- 'died before 26 June 1992' against 'dies after that date'

readings.description: ON OR AFTER. 'dies after that date' is read as the complement of 'died before 26 June 1992', so the two limbs partition the calendar and the day itself falls in the later one.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 5(9) -- the subsection is drafted as a pair of limbs evidently meant to be exhaustive of every testator

readings.foreclosure: Nothing refutes it -- a drafter writing two limbs plainly meant them to cover everybody -- and no authority found in the P2 sweep construes any of these four commencements. It is non-operative because `falls strictly after` is used uniformly and reads the words as written; the module's own instruction is that a case file falling on the boundary should be escalated rather than answered from this module.

taken.rationale: Each of these four provisions CONFERS something the general law did not -- a second route to formal validity (s 5), a saving of an attestation (s 10(3)), and the validation of an informal disposition of real estate and of a testamentary guardian (s 27) -- and a provision that confers is read no wider than its words. `falls strictly after` uses GREATER THAN and is used at every one of the four boundaries, so the choice is made once and visibly. The alternative changes the answer on exactly one day per boundary.

witnesses: `the case of a testator who died on 26 June 1992`
`the case of a testator who died on 29 May 1992`

site.anchor: `at least 2 of the attesting witnesses subscribed the will in the presence of the testator`

source.quote: the signature shall be made or acknowledged by the testator as the signature to his will or codicil in the presence of 2 or more witnesses present at the same time, and those witnesses shall subscribe the will in the presence of the testator, but no form of attestation shall be necessary.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(2)

readings.description: EVERY attesting witness must have subscribed in the testator's presence: 'those witnesses' refers back to all who were present, so a supernumerary witness who signed later and elsewhere breaks the execution.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 6(2) -- 'those witnesses shall subscribe the will in the presence of the testator', the demonstrative pointing back to the witnesses just named

readings.foreclosure: Nothing refutes it; it is the plainer reading of the demonstrative, and no Singapore authority construing s 6(2)'s subscription limb was found in the P2 sweep. It is non-operative because the encoding counts rather than quantifies universally.

readings.description: AT LEAST TWO must have subscribed in the testator's presence. Two is the number the subsection fixes ('2 or more witnesses present at the same time'), and an execution complete when the second witness subscribed is not unmade by a third.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 6(2) -- '2 or more witnesses present at the same time'

taken.rationale: The rule counts the attesting witnesses who subscribed in the testator's presence and asks whether the count is AT LEAST 2. On reading R1 a supernumerary third witness signing later, outside the testator's presence, would unmake an execution that was already complete, and the subsection nowhere makes validity turn on the conduct of a witness it does not require. The two readings differ only where there are more than two attesting witnesses.

witnesses: `the case of a legacy to one of three witnesses, another subscribing out of her sight`

site.anchor: `s 13(1) — the exception for a will made in exercise of a power of appointment`

source.quote: except a will made in exercise of a power of appointment, when the real or personal estate thereby appointed would not in default of such appointment pass to his or her heir, executor or administrator or the person entitled under the Intestate Succession Act 1967.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 13(1)

readings.description: 'when' states a FURTHER CONDITION. The exception saves an appointing will only where the appointed estate would not, in default of the appointment, fall to the statutory takers -- so the exception is a conjunction of two facts.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 13(1) -- the clause beginning 'when the real or personal estate thereby appointed would not in default of such appointment pass to' does work only if it is a condition

readings.description: 'when' is DESCRIPTIVE, equivalent to 'in which case', so every will made in exercise of a power of appointment escapes revocation by marriage and the trailing clause merely describes the usual case.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 13(1) -- 'except a will made in exercise of a power of appointment', which on its own is a complete exception

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted: 'when' is capable of the descriptive sense, and E14 records that no Singapore court has construed s 13 at all -- three differently-phrased searches produced no case on the section itself. It is non-operative because the encoding makes the clause a conjunct.

taken.rationale: Encoded as a conjunction of the two limbs. On R2 the whole of the second clause does no work, and the point of revocation by marriage is to protect the family -- which needs no protection where the appointed property would never reach them. The second limb arrives as a proved fact, because whether the estate 'would not in default of such appointment pass to' those takers is a question about a counterfactual instrument rather than about this estate.

witnesses: `the case of a will made under a power whose appointed estate passes in default, Amrita marrying Gita`
`the case of an appointing will, Amrita marrying Gita in 2018`
notes: E14 is a checked negative and is cross-referenced for that reason: it establishes that no Singapore authority reads down s 13, which is why both readings are still on the table. It does not settle the fork and this entry does not claim it does.

site.anchor: `s 13(2) — the will is expressed to be made in contemplation of this marriage`

source.quote: Notwithstanding subsection (1), where a will made on or after 29 August 1938 is expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage, the will shall not be revoked by the solemnisation of the marriage contemplated; and this subsection shall apply notwithstanding that the marriage contemplated may be the first, second or subsequent marriage of a person lawfully practising polygamy.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 13(2)

readings.description: The saving applies only to a marriage SHOWN TO BE the marriage contemplated. Where the will is expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage but does not identify the intended spouse, the saving does not apply and s 13(1) revokes.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 13(2) -- 'the will shall not be revoked by the solemnisation of the marriage contemplated', and of no other

Wills Act 1838 s 13(2) -- 'the first, second or subsequent marriage of a person lawfully practising polygamy', which puts the subsection in a cohort where more than one marriage is contemplated by the drafter

readings.description: Where the testator married once and the will contemplates a marriage, that marriage is the one contemplated: identification is an inference from the facts rather than a requirement of the subsection.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 13(2) -- the subsection requires only that the will be 'expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage', without requiring the intended spouse to be named

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted, and defensible on a single-marriage file; E14 records that no Singapore court has construed s 13. It is non-operative because the encoding requires the recorded reference for the intended spouse to match the spouse of the marriage in question, and a NOTHING reference makes the conjunct FALSE.

taken.rationale: family-domain.l4 carries two fields -- that the will is expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage, and a MAYBE STRING reference for the person with whom the marriage contemplated was to be solemnised -- and expressly leaves the NOTHING case to this module. The rule folds NOTHING to FALSE. R2's premise, that there was only one marriage, is exactly what the subsection's closing words about a person lawfully practising polygamy forbid assuming.

notes: No fixture in the module sets `it is expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage` TRUE with the intended-spouse reference absent, so the two readings are not separated by any case file that exists. `unassessed` rather than `none`: the readings would diverge on such a file, and building it is a P6 job.

site.anchor: `was living on`

source.quote: Where any person being a child or other issue of the testator to whom any real or personal estate shall be devised or bequeathed for any estate or interest not determinable at or before the death of that person shall die in the lifetime of the testator leaving issue, and any such issue of that person shall be living at the time of the death of the testator, that devise or bequest shall not lapse, but shall take effect as if the death of that person had happened immediately after the death of the testator, unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 26

readings.description: A person recorded as having died on the testator's own date of death is NOT shown to have been living at the time of that death. The comparison is strict.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 26 -- 'shall be living at the time of the death of the testator', a moment and not a day, and an exception whose beneficiary must make it out

readings.description: He is taken to have been living unless the contrary is shown, because a date is not a moment and dying on the same day is consistent with surviving by hours.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 26 -- the phrase fixes a moment, and a shared date leaves the order of two deaths within that day undetermined rather than decided against the claimant

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted -- it is the reading a commorientes rule would need -- but non-operative because family-domain.l4 records a DATE of death and no time, so R2 would have the module assert survivorship on no evidence. The module's instruction is that a commorientes case is not answerable from a date and should be escalated.

taken.rationale: `was living on` returns TRUE for a living person, `Day (date of death) GREATER THAN Day (the day)` for a person who died on a known date, and FALSE where the death is undated. s 26 is an exception and its beneficiary must make it out; the ontology records no time of day, so the strict comparison is the only one supported by the facts the module holds.

notes: The same convention is applied one Act over at F-ISA-A19 for ISA s 7's 'surviving', with the same allocation of the burden and for the same reason -- the ontology holds dates, not moments. The two were reached independently and agree.

site.anchor: `s 28(2) — whether the application for rectification is in time`

source.quote: Except with the permission of a court, an application for an order under subsection (1) must be made no later than 6 months after the date on which a grant authorising the administration of the testator’s estate is first made.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 28(2)

readings.description: The six months runs FROM a grant, so before any grant has been made the period has not begun and an application cannot be late.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 28(2) -- the subsection states a latest date and nothing else; it fixes no earliest date and imposes no precondition on applying

readings.description: The subsection presupposes a grant, so an application made before one is premature and falls outside s 28(2) altogether.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 28(2) -- the period is measured from 'the date on which a grant authorising the administration of the testator’s estate is first made', which presupposes such a grant

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted; the presupposition argument is available on the words. Non-operative because reading it that way would have the module report a bar the section does not create.

taken.rationale: `Whether an application for rectification is within the time allowed by section 28(2)` gives the case its own member, `within the time allowed, no grant authorising the administration of the testator’s estate having yet been made`, rather than folding it into the ordinary in-time answer -- so a reader can see that the case was decided and how.

witnesses: `an application to rectify, no grant having been made`

site.anchor: `s 15 — the will has been revoked`

source.quote: No will or codicil, or any part thereof, shall be revoked otherwise than —

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 15

readings.description: Partial revocation is a SEPARATE question, asked of each part of the will, and is not answered by the whole-instrument decision at all.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 15 -- 'No will or codicil, or any part thereof', the Act itself distinguishing the instrument from its parts
Wills Act 1838 s 17(2) -- the Act's own recognition of a will 'partly revoked, and afterwards wholly revoked', a distinction that presupposes parts

readings.description: Partial revocation can be folded into the whole: a will any part of which is revoked is treated as revoked for the purposes of this decision.
readings.rejection_rationale: It would report an instrument as revoked on facts that revoke only a clause of it, which s 15's own words ('or any part thereof') keep apart. The encoding takes the opposite course and answers only the instrument-level question.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 15

taken.rationale: TAKEN AND NOT ENCODED, which is the honest description. Nothing in the shared ontology divides a will into parts -- there is no clause, no paragraph, no severable provision -- so a per-part answer would have nothing to range over. The one place partial revocation surfaces is s 17(2), whose fact `partly revoked, and afterwards wholly revoked` is recorded and used. A file in which only part of a will was revoked is outside what this module can say, and the decision returning FALSE must NOT be read as an answer to it.

notes: The same limit bites again at s 5(3)(b)-(d), whose 'so far as' paragraphs are reported under their own outcome rather than poured into a whole-will verdict, and at F-WA-A10 on s 16(1). Three provisions, one missing part-of-a-will ontology.

site.anchor: `the will is duly executed without the attestation of any such person`

source.quote: The attestation of a will by a person to whom or to whose spouse there is given or made any disposition as is described in subsection (1) shall be disregarded for the purposes of that subsection if the will is duly executed without his attestation and without that of any other such person.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 10(3)

readings.description: 'duly executed' imports THE WHOLE OF s 6(1)-(2), re-asked with the benefiting witnesses struck out: writing, signature, acknowledgement before two witnesses and subscription.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 16(2) -- 'deemed to be duly executed', used of compliance with s 6 as a whole, which fixes the Act's own sense of the phrase

readings.description: Only the ATTESTATION requirements are re-asked; the writing and signature limbs are unaffected by who attested, so they need not be re-tested.
readings.rejection_rationale: On this reading an unsigned will with three witnesses could satisfy s 10(3) while failing s 6 -- saving an attestation for a will that has none to save. 'Duly executed' is the Act's own phrase for compliance with s 6 as a whole.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 10(3)

taken.rationale: The rule restates the whole of s 6 -- in writing; signed at the foot or end by the testator or by another at his direction, or deemed valid in position under s 6(3); the signature made or acknowledged before 2 or more witnesses counting only non-benefiting ones; and at least two non-benefiting witnesses subscribing in the testator's presence. The readings differ only where the will fails s 6 for a reason having nothing to do with the witnesses, in which case the gift falls with the will anyway.

site.anchor: `s 16(1) — the alteration is valid and has effect`

source.quote: No obliteration, interlineation or other alteration made in any will after the execution thereof shall be valid or have any effect except so far as the words or effect of the will before such alteration shall not be apparent, unless the alteration shall be executed in the like manner as by this Act is required for the execution of the will.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 16(1)

readings.description: PRO TANTO. 'except so far as' operates to the extent that the earlier words are illegible, so a partial obliteration is partly good and partly bad.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 16(1) -- 'except so far as the words or effect of the will before such alteration shall not be apparent', which is quantitative language

readings.foreclosure: This is the ORTHODOX reading and the encoding does not contradict it -- it declines to compute it. Nothing in the shared ontology divides an alteration into the legible and illegible parts of what it struck out, so there is nothing for a pro tanto answer to range over.

readings.description: ALL OR NOTHING for a given alteration: the alteration either takes effect or does not, and 'so far as' is read as a condition rather than a measure.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 16(1) -- the prohibition is stated of an 'obliteration, interlineation or other alteration' as a unit, and s 16(2)'s deeming operates on the same unit

taken.rationale: The decision returns a BOOLEAN about one alteration, as a disjunction of the subsection's two independent escapes: that the earlier words are not apparent, or that the alteration was itself executed in the required manner (including the s 16(2) deeming). A case in which an obliteration is only partly effective is outside what this module can say. This is the same limit as F-WA-A8 records on s 15's 'or any part thereof', and it is recorded rather than hidden because the orthodox reading is the one not computed.

site.anchor: `s 7(1) — the appointment made by the will in exercise of a power is invalid for want of execution in the manner required by this Act`

source.quote: No appointment made by will, in exercise of any power, shall be valid, unless the will is executed in the manner required by this Act.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7(1)
Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 5(1) -- 'This section shall take effect notwithstanding any other provisions of this Act.'
Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 5(3)(d) -- '(d) a will so far as it exercises a power of appointment, if the execution of the will conformed to the law governing the essential validity of the power.'

readings.description: s 7(1) STILL BITES. 'executed in the manner required by this Act' means s 6, whereas s 5 speaks of a will 'treated as properly executed' -- a different phrase for a different thing -- so a will saved by s 5 alone still makes no valid appointment.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 7(1) against s 5(3) -- the Act uses 'executed in the manner required by this Act' and 'treated as properly executed' in different places, and the difference is not obviously accidental

readings.foreclosure: It may well be right ABOUT THE PHRASE and still wrong about the RESULT, which is why it is arguable rather than rejected: a notwithstanding clause does not redefine another section's words, it stops that section taking effect against the one it protects. It is non-operative because on the encoding it produced a contradiction -- see the taken rationale -- and it was previously stated as settled in a note on s 7(2), which is the state this repair corrected.

readings.description: s 7(1) CANNOT BITE where s 5 is made out as to the appointment: s 5(1)'s notwithstanding stops every other provision of the Act operating against s 5, and pronouncing the appointment invalid for want of execution is exactly that.

citations.cite: Wills Act 1838 s 5(1) -- 'This section shall take effect notwithstanding any other provisions of this Act.'
Wills Act 1838 s 5(3)(d) -- 'a will so far as it exercises a power of appointment'

taken.rationale: `AND NOT (s 5 — the will is treated as properly executed so far as it exercises a power of appointment)` is a conjunct of the s 7(1) rule. THE FORK WAS FOUND BY A CONTRADICTION, not by argument alone (ROUND 2, R2): on the case file `the case of an appointing will conforming only to the law governing the essential validity of the power` the module reported both that the will WAS treated as properly executed so far as it exercises the appointment and that the appointment was invalid for want of execution. Under the affirmative rule this replaced, the same case merely returned FALSE -- uninformative rather than contradictory -- so the defect arrived with the polarity repair that preceded it. The readings differ only where s 5 is made out and s 6 is not, which is the foreign-execution case s 5 was inserted for.

witnesses: `the case of an appointing will conforming only to the law governing the essential validity of the power`

site.anchor: `section 2 — nothing in this Act applies to the estate`

source.quote: Nothing in this Act shall apply to the estate of any Muslim or shall affect any rules of the Muslim law in respect of the distribution of the estate of any such person.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 2

readings.description: Whether the deceased was a Muslim is a fact about him ARRIVING ALREADY CONSTRUED, decided outside this Act by whoever supplies the facts.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 2 -- the section supplies no test of who is a Muslim and names no date at which the question is asked

readings.description: It is a question THIS ACT decides, so the Act carries an implicit test -- profession of the faith at death, or registration, or the personal law by which the deceased lived.
readings.rejection_rationale: A section that supplies no test cannot be read as creating one. s 2 is a single sentence of exclusion; every candidate test would have to be imported from outside the Act, which is the opposite of the reading it would support.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 2

taken.rationale: `section 2 — nothing in this Act applies to the estate` reads `Deceased person`'s `a Muslim` and nothing else, so the fact supplier bears the whole question -- who is a Muslim, and as at when. THE COST IS PRECISE: the P2 sweep records (E23) that the harder problem sits one level down, in what 'estate' denotes for a deceased Muslim under AMLA s 112(1), and that ISA s 2 excludes 'any Muslim' with no domicile qualifier while AMLA s 112(1) applies only to a 'Muslim person domiciled in Singapore', leaving a non-domiciled Muslim outside both regimes on a literal reading. That gap is visible on the face of the two texts and no case resolving it was found. This encoding does not close it; the boolean simply routes the estate out.

notes: divergence 'none' in the sense the schema gives it: the field arrives pre-construed, so the encoding cannot tell the readings apart even though they say different things.

site.anchor: `section 3 — a “child” within the meaning of this Act`

source.quote: “child” means a legitimate child and includes any child adopted by virtue of an order of court under any written law for the time being in force in Singapore, Malaysia or Brunei Darussalam;

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 3

readings.description: The three named jurisdictions are EXHAUSTIVE: an adoption order made anywhere else does not answer the definition, however regular.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 3 -- 'under any written law for the time being in force in Singapore, Malaysia or Brunei Darussalam', three countries named where one general phrase would have sufficed

readings.description: The list is ILLUSTRATIVE of adoption orders generally, the drafter naming the jurisdictions whose orders were then familiar rather than shutting out the rest.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 3 -- the limb is introduced by 'includes', the Act's inclusive verb, not by 'means'

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted, and E16 is explicit that the point remains open: Lim Weipin recited s 3's confinement to orders of court under written law in force in Singapore, Malaysia or Brunei Darussalam but DID NOT DECIDE whether a foreign adoption order qualifies. It is non-operative because the ontology's boolean carries the whole phrase, three jurisdictions included, so a fact supplier answering it truthfully cannot record a foreign order as satisfying it.

taken.rationale: The adoption limb is encoded as `Child`'s `adopted by that person by virtue of an order of court under any written law for the time being in force in Singapore, Malaysia or Brunei Darussalam` -- the field name carries the three jurisdictions, so the restriction is in the encoding and not merely in a comment. notes: E15 and E16 confirm that s 3 is exhaustive AS TO LEGITIMACY -- the CA in AAG v Estate of AAH proceeded on that footing, and Lim Weipin applied it as the gate on standing -- but neither reaches the jurisdictional question this entry is about, and the module treats the legitimacy limb as plain rather than as a fork. site.anchor: `the intestate leaves issue` AKA `there are descendants`

source.quote: “issue” includes children and the descendants of deceased children.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 3
Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7 rule 5 -- 'If there are no descendants, the parent or parents of the intestate shall take the estate'

readings.description: 'issue' (rules 1, 2, 3) and 'descendants' (rules 5-8) are COEXTENSIVE, so rule 5's 'no descendants' is rule 2's 'no issue' asked again. The gate is stated as surviving descendants who take or are represented under rule 3.

Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rule 3 Proviso No. (2) -- 'Descendants of the intestate to the remotest degree stand in the place of their parent or other ancestor'

readings.description: 'descendants' is the WIDER word, catching a grandchild whose own parent is alive -- a person who takes nothing under rule 3 but who would still keep the parents out under rule 5.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rules 5, 6, 7, 8 -- 'descendants', a word the Act nowhere defines

Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 4(1) -- the movables of a Singapore domiciliary are referred to Singapore law without regard to where they are

Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 5(b) -- 'domiciled outside Singapore and possessed beneficially of immovable property situated in Singapore'

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7 rule 3

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(a)

readings.rejection_rationale: It would drop an undated child silently out of a distribution. citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 6(a)

taken.rationale: `actually born in the lifetime of the intestate` folds a NOTHING date of birth to TRUE. It is the one place in this module where an absent fact is resolved in the claimant's FAVOUR, and it is stated as such: F-ISA-A5, F-ISA-A8, F-ISA-A17 and F-ISA-A20 all run the other way.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7 rule 4
Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7 rule 1 -- 'If an intestate dies leaving a surviving spouse, no issue and no parent'

readings.description: 'parent' means a parent WHO SURVIVES the intestate, the word 'surviving' being carried over from the spouse limb of the same sentence.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rule 6 -- 'If there are no surviving spouse, descendants or parents', where the Act runs the same class through the word 'surviving'

readings.rejection_rationale: It makes rule 1's 'no parent' nearly a dead letter -- everyone has two parents -- and contradicts rules 6 to 8, which run the same class through the phrase 'If there are no surviving spouse, descendants or parents'. A dead parent cannot take an estate.

A SECOND AND NARROWER CHOICE RIDES ON THE ONTOLOGY RATHER THAN ON THE ACT and is recorded with it: a NOTHING in `the father of the deceased` means the parent is NOT IN EVIDENCE, not that he is dead, and a parent not in evidence cannot be shown to survive -- so he does not take. site.anchor: `rule 6 — the stocks of brothers and sisters between which the estate is shared in equal portions`

source.quote: If there are no surviving spouse, descendants or parents, the brothers and sisters and children of deceased brothers or sisters of the intestate shall share the estate in equal portions between the brothers and sisters and the children of any deceased brother or sister shall take according to their stocks the share which the deceased brother or sister would have taken.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7 rule 6

readings.description: The ranking is applied to the CLASS OF STOCKS, at the sibling level: a half-blood brother is excluded while a whole-blood brother's children still represent him.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rule 6 -- the estate is shared 'in equal portions between the brothers and sisters', and only then do children take 'the share which the deceased brother or sister would have taken'

readings.description: The ranking is applied to the INDIVIDUAL TAKERS, so a half-blood brother (second degree) would outrank a whole-blood nephew (third degree) who is present in the same distribution.
readings.rejection_rationale: Rule 6 divides among the siblings and lets the children take derivatively, so the class s 6(b) orders is the class of siblings. On this reading the ranking would be applied to a mixed-degree class that rule 6 never treats as one.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 6(b) -- 'related to him in the same degree', which presupposes that the class being ordered is of one degree

taken.rationale: `rule 6 — the stocks of brothers and sisters between which the estate is shared in equal portions` applies `section 6(b) — those of the whole blood, the half blood ranking immediately after them` to the sibling list and to nothing further down.

source.quote: and such persons as legally represent those children, in case any of those children be then dead

readings.description: A child who predeceased leaving no surviving descendant is NOT A STOCK AT ALL, so the fund is divided among the stocks that do take. Three children, one of whom died childless, gives one half each to the other two.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rule 3 -- 'in case any of those children be then dead', which pairs the dead child with the persons who represent him and so contemplates a representative

source.quote: there shall be no distinction between those who are related to a person deceased through his father and those who are related to him through his mother nor between those who were actually born in his lifetime and those who at the date of his death were only conceived in the womb but who have subsequently been born alive; and

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(a)

readings.description: The paragraph settles NOTHING about membership. It is drafted as a rule against distinctions -- 'there shall be no distinction between ... nor between ...' -- and on its face levels two classes rather than shutting anybody out, so a person in neither class is excluded (if at all) by the general law and not by this paragraph.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 6(a) -- 'For the purposes of distribution — (a) there shall be no distinction between', which is the grammar of an equalising rule and not of an eligibility rule

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted, and it is the more literal reading of the paragraph's grammar. It is non-operative because on it THIS ACT HAS NO ANSWER AT ALL for a child conceived after the death -- nothing else in it excludes him, so he would take as though he had been alive throughout.

readings.description: The two classes it names are EXHAUSTIVE of the persons from among whom takers are drawn, so a person conceived after the intestate's death is outside them and takes nothing.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 6(a) -- 'those who were actually born in his lifetime' and 'those who at the date of his death were only conceived in the womb but who have subsequently been born alive', an enumeration given full effect

taken.rationale: `the person survives the intestate and is within the classes section 6(a) names` conjoins survivorship with the s 6(a) test and is read by EVERY class of taker. THE PART THAT WAS A DEFECT RATHER THAN A CHOICE: an earlier draft applied the test to only two of the six classes, so a posthumously-conceived brother took the whole estate under rule 6 while a posthumously-conceived child on identical facts took nothing under rule 3. Case 17a exhibits the sibling case that used to escape it.

witnesses: `case 17a — a brother conceived after the intestate's death`
`case 17d — an uncle conceived after the intestate's death`
`case 17f — a niece in the womb at the death, and a nephew conceived after it`

site.anchor: `the person survives the intestate` against `actually born in the lifetime of the intestate`

source.quote: If a person dies intestate after 2 June 1967, he being at the time of his death —

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 5 -- 'he being at the time of his death', a moment
Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(a) -- 'actually born in his lifetime', a moment

readings.description: Resolve the unknown moment AGAINST the person asserting it: a birth or death sharing the intestate's date of death is not shown to fall on the favourable side.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rule 3 -- 'in case any of those children be then dead', survivorship being what the claimant must establish

readings.description: Resolve it IN FAVOUR of inclusion, so a person born or dying on the intestate's date of death is within the class.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 6(a) -- the paragraph's purpose is to widen rather than narrow the class of takers, levelling two distinctions rather than drawing them

taken.rationale: SPLIT BY DIRECTION, ON PURPOSE. R1 for SURVIVORSHIP (`the person survives the intestate` compares GREATER THAN, so a claimant recorded as having died on the intestate's own date of death is not shown to have survived him) and R2 for BIRTH (`actually born in the lifetime of the intestate` compares AT MOST, so a claimant born on that date IS taken to have been born in the lifetime). The two comparisons are strict and inclusive respectively, matching F-ISA-A8 and F-ISA-A9. `taken` can name only one reading and names R1, the survivorship half; the birth half takes R2 and the boundary is asserted from both sides beside case 17.

witnesses: §§§ `Case 17c — AMBIGUITY A19: the same-day boundary, from both sides`
notes: The witness is named by its §§§ heading because case 17c is a block of assertions over several fixtures rather than a single named constructor.

The schema's `taken` holds one reading, and this fork genuinely takes different readings in the two places it arises. Recorded here rather than split into two entries, so the 1:1 map with the module's own register survives; a reader who needs the birth half must read this note and not the `taken` field alone.

site.anchor: `section 10 — the value of the part of his property so disposed of`

source.quote: the provisions of this Act shall have effect as respects the part of his property not so disposed of

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 10

readings.description: Subtract the WHOLE value beneficially disposed of from the Singapore fund, wherever the disposed property is.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 10 -- 'the part of his property not so disposed of', with no words of situs anywhere in the section

readings.description: Subtract only SO MUCH of it as falls on Singapore property, since the fund it comes off is confined to Singapore by s 5 and foreign assets stand available to satisfy a foreign legacy.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 5(a) and s 5(b) -- both limbs reach only property 'situated in Singapore', so the subtrahend and the fund are measured over different bodies of property

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted -- it is arguably the better reading -- but NOT EXPRESSIBLE in the model at all: `Disposition` in family-domain.l4 carries a donee, a kind and a value and NO situs, so the encoding cannot say out of which property a legacy is satisfied.

taken.rationale: TAKEN FOR WANT OF AN ALTERNATIVE RATHER THAN ON THE WORDS, which is why it is recorded here rather than argued. The whole disposed value reduces the Singapore fund pound for pound although foreign assets stand available to satisfy it. R1 can only UNDER-state the fund, never over-state it, which is the same allocation of the burden as F-ISA-A5, F-ISA-A7 and F-ISA-A17. If a later ontology gives a disposition a situs, `section 10 — the part of his property not so disposed of` is the line that changes.

witnesses: `case 15c — a will beside immovable property outside Singapore`

site.anchor: `rule 6 — this brother or sister shares, or has children who take according to their stocks`

source.quote: the brothers and sisters and children of deceased brothers or sisters of the intestate shall share the estate in equal portions between the brothers and sisters

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7 rule 6

readings.description: NO: representation runs only from a DEAD sibling. A sibling who is alive but outside the classes s 6(a) names is neither a taker nor a stock, and his children take nothing.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rule 6 -- 'deceased' three times in one sentence: 'children of deceased brothers or sisters', 'the children of any deceased brother or sister', 'the share which the deceased brother or sister would have taken'
Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 rule 3 -- 'in case any of those children be then dead', which already reads representation as running from death

readings.description: YES: s 6(a) deems him not to have been in being at the relevant moment, which is the same thing as a predecease, so his children stand in his place exactly as they would if he had died first.
readings.rejection_rationale: It requires 'deceased' to mean 'not entitled', a meaning the drafter had no occasion to give it in 1967 and did not. It also breaks the parity with rule 3, whose stock test already reads representation as running from death.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 6(a)

taken.rationale: TAKEN ON THE WORDS, and it restores the parity that F-ISA-A18 is about. An earlier version of this decision took R2, so a posthumously-conceived BROTHER's children took the whole estate while a posthumously-conceived CHILD's children, on identical facts, took nothing -- the same asymmetry between rules 3 and 6 one generation down, which survived the repair that fixed A18 because no fixture then had an excluded sibling WITH children. Case 17e is the fork itself ($1,000,000 to the Government against $1,000,000 to the excluded brother's daughter); case 17g is a real deceased brother, whose child does take.

witnesses: `case 17e — a brother conceived after the death, leaving a surviving child`
`case 17g — a brother who predeceased, leaving the same surviving child`

site.anchor: `survives`

source.quote: no executor survives the testator;

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 13(1)(c)

readings.description: Survivorship is a fact to be PROVED. A person known to be dead but on an unknown date is not shown to have survived anybody, and a testator whose own death is undated cannot be outlived.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 13(1) -- the five limbs are a gate that OPENS a grant of letters of administration with the will annexed, and a limb not proved is a limb not made out

readings.description: Survivorship is PRESUMED from the order in which the facts were recorded, or from the person being alive at the date of the application.
readings.rejection_rationale: It would let an unproved fact open the gate. s 13(1) confers a jurisdiction to grant, and a provision that confers is not satisfied by a limb nobody has established.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 13(1)(c)

taken.rationale: `survives` returns TRUE for the living, FALSE for a person dead on an unknown date, and compares dates otherwise -- returning FALSE if the OTHER person's death is undated too. The same discipline governs s 55(1)(f)'s six-month clock, which cannot be started from a date not in evidence, and the s 18(4) next-of-kin filter, where a relative not shown to have survived drops out of both the numerator and the denominator.

witnesses: `Tan Ah Kow, the date of death not known`
`the Tan intestacy, the date of death not known, the administrator having died`

site.anchor: `is an infant on`

source.quote: No probate or letters of administration shall be granted to a person while he is an infant.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 21(1)

readings.description: Infancy is NOT ESTABLISHED where the date of majority is not in evidence, so the s 21(1) bar does not bite and no minority is found for s 6(2).

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 6(3) -- 'The court in granting letters of administration may act on such prima facie evidence, furnished by the applicant or any other person, as to whether or not there is a minority or life interest, as may be prescribed by rules made under any written law for the time being in force relating to the courts.'

readings.description: The protective provisions -- s 6(2), s 29(8)(a), s 63 -- should ASSUME INFANCY until majority is proved, since they exist to protect the infant and the cost of a wrong answer is asymmetric.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 29(8)(a) -- security is required where 'the person for whose use and benefit the grant is made is an infant', a protective provision whose failure mode is one-sided

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted -- it is the safer default for a drafter, and the module says so. It is non-operative because the encoding folds a NOTHING majority date to FALSE; a consumer who wants R2 adopts it by supplying the date.

taken.rationale: `is an infant on` folds a NOTHING date of majority to FALSE, uniformly. s 6(3) is what lets that be taken without loss: the Act itself routes the EVIDENTIAL question to the court and to rules of court, so a module answering it from silence would be substituting for a forum the Act names. WHAT THE FOLD COSTS, STATED PLAINLY: an unproved age passes the s 21(1) bar. The encoding does NOT put the burden of proving full age on the person propounding the grant -- on the three states of the evidence (proved infant, proved adult, not in evidence) the bar bites on the first only -- and a drafter who wants the burden the other way must change this decision and not merely the phrasing of s 21(1). THIS IS ONE OF THREE ANSWERS THE CORPUS GIVES THE SAME EVIDENTIAL QUESTION: see F-WA-A1 (a third enum value) and F-GIA-17 (NOTHING propagated). Each is argued on its own Act and none is said to be wrong.

witnesses: `a PAA person of unknown age` "Unknown" "unk", asserted NOT to be barred by `s 21(1) — no probate or letters of administration shall be granted to a person while he is an infant`
notes: E1 is cross-referenced because it is the strongest written-law anchor for the number the PAA lacks: Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024 P.6 r 24 makes a grant during infancy run 'until he or she attains 21 years of age', and neither s 21 nor the s 2 interpretation section defines 'infant'. It bears on WHAT the age is; it does not touch the evidential fork this entry states, which is what to do when the date is missing whatever the age.

site.anchor: `the classes from which the next of kin are drawn`

source.quote: letters of administration may be granted to the husband or widow or next of kin or any of them;

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 18(4)(a)

readings.description: 'next of kin' means the classes to whom the Intestate Succession Act 1967 distributes on an intestacy -- issue, parents, brothers and sisters and their issue, grandparents, uncles and aunts -- taken as ONE FLAT CLASS.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 18(4)(b) -- 'it shall be in the discretion of the court to grant them to any one or more of such persons', which presupposes a class wider than one rung
Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 18(4)(d)(i) -- 'the greater number of such next of kin', a count that a single-rung reading would make turn on the accident of which rung is occupied

readings.description: It means the NEAREST such class only, the Intestate Succession Act's ranking being carried across into the grant.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 7 -- the rules are an ordered ladder in which a nearer class shuts a remoter one out

Toh Seok Kheng v Huang Huiqun [2010] SGHC 308, [2011] 1 SLR 737 at [23]-[24], applied in Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh [2025] SGHC 112 at [39] -- priority to a grant follows priority of beneficial entitlement to the estate under ISA s 7

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted, and it has authority pulling towards it -- but the authority is about PRIORITY among applicants, not about MEMBERSHIP of the class, and this Act does not import the Intestate Succession Act's ranking in terms. Non-operative because `the classes from which the next of kin are drawn` returns the classes flat.

taken.rationale: The Act uses the phrase three times and never defines it. s 18(4)(b)'s discretion and s 18(4)(d)(i)'s count both read more naturally on a flat class. THE SPOUSE IS NOT IN THE LIST: s 18(4)(a) names 'the husband or widow' separately from 'next of kin', so folding the spouse in would make the Act's own disjunction redundant. A PREDECEASED RELATIVE IS NOT NEXT OF KIN either, and the survivorship filter is F-PAA-A1's -- an earlier draft filtered the spouse limb and not this one, so a child who died before his father was still counted and his silence defeated the unanimous wish of the living. WHAT A3 DOES NOT DECIDE is who FILLS those classes; that is F-PAA-A12.

notes: E19 IS CROSS-REFERENCED AND IS NOT TREATED AS SETTLING THIS FORK, and the distinction matters. Toh Seok Kheng and Cheng Tze Tzuen establish that priority to a grant follows priority of beneficial entitlement under ISA s 7 -- spouse ahead of parent, spouse ahead of child. That is an ORDER among applicants, not a restriction on who is next of kin, and this module encodes no such order: `the classes from which the next of kin are drawn` returns them flat and s 18(4)(b)'s discretion is left as the Act leaves it. So the authority supplies a ranking the encoding does not implement. E19's own disposition note anticipates this link and declines to claim it because no fork register then existed; the link is made here, as a bearing and not as a settlement.

The previous three-Act register (denovo F7) treated the same authority as SETTLING a differently-stated fork -- whether s 18(4)(a)'s list is a free-standing order independent of ISA s 7 -- and that encoding derived its grant order from the ISA classes. That is a different question from this one and a different encoding; the two registers are not versions of each other.

site.anchor: `s 6(2) — there is a minority`

source.quote: Letters of administration shall, if there is a minority or if a life interest arises under the will, be granted either to a trust corporation, with or without an individual, or to not less than 2 individuals.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(2)

readings.description: A minority among ANYONE CONCERNED in the estate -- an infant beneficiary, but also an infant executor or an infant otherwise entitled to a grant.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 6(2) -- 'if there is a minority', unqualified, where s 6(4) two subsections later says 'the minority of a beneficiary'

readings.description: A minority among the BENEFICIARIES only, the mischief being an infant's property administered by one person.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 6(4) -- 'during the minority of a beneficiary or the subsistence of a life interest', the Act's own narrower formula

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted; s 6(4)'s narrower words two subsections later are a real argument that the same was meant in s 6(2). Non-operative because the predicate reads `the infants concerned in the estate` -- but a case file that wants R2 gets it by listing only the infant beneficiaries there, which is why this fork is delegated rather than resolved.

taken.rationale: `s 6(2) — there is a minority` asks whether ANY member of `the infants concerned in the estate` is an infant on the date, and the encoding cannot check who was put on that list. The field's NAME carries R1 -- anyone concerned, not beneficiaries only -- and the module states expressly that a case file wanting R2 states only the infant beneficiaries in it. So the reading is defaulted by the ontology and settled by the fact supplier. s 6(2) is drafted without the qualifier s 6(4) has, the difference is not obviously accidental, and R1 is the wider protection. NOTE WHAT IS NOT PART OF THIS FORK: s 6(4)'s 'the minority of a beneficiary' is a NARROWER predicate of its own, `s 6(4) — there is a minority of a beneficiary`, and this entry rules on s 6(2) only.

witnesses: `the Ong testacy, an infant executor, Chan administering`

site.anchor: `s 6(2) — the grant is one of the grants section 6(2) governs`

source.quote: Letters of administration shall, if there is a minority or if a life interest arises under the will, be granted either to a trust corporation, with or without an individual, or to not less than 2 individuals.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(2)

readings.description: s 6(2) reaches BOTH kinds of grant -- letters of administration simpliciter and letters with the will annexed -- because its own second limb ('if a life interest arises under the will') presupposes a will, and a will case is the will-annexed case.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 6(2) -- 'or if a life interest arises under the will'

readings.description: It reaches letters of administration SIMPLICITER ONLY, s 2 defining the two grants as separate terms.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 21(2) -- 'letters of administration with or without the will annexed', showing that the Act says both in as many words when it means both

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted: s 2's separate definitions and s 21(2)'s explicit both-kinds formula are real. Non-operative because it would leave the life-interest limb with no work to do, and because the encoding admits both kinds of grant to the predicate.

taken.rationale: `s 6(2) — the grant is one of the grants section 6(2) governs` is a disjunction over the two kinds. R2 would empty half the subsection. THE SAME FORK IS ASKED AGAIN OF s 30 AT F-PAA-A11 and answered the same way for a DIFFERENT reason, because this reasoning turns on s 6(2)'s life-interest limb and does not carry. s 29(8) asks it a third time and is NOT a fork, because s 29(7) answers it in terms: the duty s 29(8) excuses is imposed 'in the case of administrations whether with or without the will annexed'.

witnesses: `the Ong testacy with a life interest` under `letters with the will annexed to Chan alone`

site.anchor: `s 13(1)(b) — the executors are legally incapable of acting as such, or have renounced the right to act as such`

source.quote: the executor or all the executors appointed by will are legally incapable of acting as such, or have renounced the right to act as such;

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 13(1)(b)

readings.description: PER EXECUTOR: every appointed executor is disqualified, each by one route or the other, so a will with one incapable executor and one who has renounced satisfies the limb.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 13(1) -- the mischief of the section is that no appointed executor can take the grant, and the five limbs between them exist to supply a route to one

readings.description: PER CLASS: either all of them are legally incapable, or all of them have renounced, and a mixed case satisfies neither branch of the disjunction.
readings.rejection_rationale: It would leave a will whose executors are disqualified in different ways with no route to a grant at all -- which limb (b) plainly exists to prevent.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 13(1)(b)

taken.rationale: `s 13(1)(b) — this executor is disqualified` is per-executor and takes either route, and the limb is `all` of the appointed executors being disqualified in that sense.

witnesses: `the will whose executors are disqualified`
`the will one of whose executors is disqualified`

site.anchor: `s 18(1) — the person has died intestate`

source.quote: When a person has died intestate, the court may grant letters of administration of his estate.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 18(1)

readings.description: A person dies intestate for s 18 when there is NO WILL AT ALL, so a partial intestacy is not s 18's case: the estate takes letters with the will annexed under s 13.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 2 -- the two grants are defined by what they authorise: administration of 'an intestate’s estate in accordance with law' against administration 'in compliance with the directions contained in his will'

readings.description: The Intestate Succession Act's inclusive definition is carried across, so a will disposing of part engages s 18 as to the rest.

citations.cite: Intestate Succession Act 1967 s 3 -- '“intestate” includes any person who leaves a will but dies intestate as to some beneficial interest in his property'

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted: the neighbouring Act defines the very word inclusively, and this Act does not define it at all. Non-operative because an estate with a will has directions to comply with, so it takes the s 13 grant; and because that Act's definition is about DISTRIBUTION, which is its subject and not this one's.

taken.rationale: `s 18(1) — the person has died intestate` is `isNothing (d's the will)`. NOTE THE SHAPE OF THE DIVERGENCE FROM F-PAA-A3 AND F-PAA-A12: this module DECLINES the neighbouring Act's definition here and TAKES it there, and the difference is that 'next of kin' is a phrase this Act construes by reference to the other while 'died intestate' is a phrase this Act's own s 2 supplies content for. The two Acts can differ here without contradiction.

site.anchor: `s 18(4)(d)(i) — the next of kin, or the greater number of such next of kin, so desire`

source.quote: the next of kin of any person dying intestate, or the greater number of such next of kin, so desire; or

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 18(4)(d)(i)

readings.description: A MAJORITY: more than half of the next of kin so desire. The unanimous case satisfies this a fortiori, so the first limb of the disjunction adds nothing operative and reads as emphasis.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 18(4)(d)(i) -- 'the greater number of such next of kin', measured against the class it names

readings.description: The larger of two OPPOSING GROUPS: more of them desire it than oppose it, so next of kin who express no view are not counted in the denominator.
readings.rejection_rationale: `Person` carries a single boolean and so records no third, abstaining state; on that shape the two readings differ only in the denominator, and the majority reading is the one that cannot be gamed by adding silent relatives.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 18(4)(d)(i)

taken.rationale: The count of those so desiring, TIMES 2, must be GREATER THAN the count of the next of kin. The limb is FALSE where there are no next of kin at all, because 'the greater number of such next of kin' presupposes some.

witnesses: `the Tan intestacy`
`Tan Ah Kow, the children so desiring`
notes: E19 bears here for the same reason it bears on F-PAA-A3 -- it is about the same class -- and for the same reason it does not settle this one: it supplies an order of priority among applicants, not a rule for counting who desires a grant to a third person.

site.anchor: `s 25(1) — death of one of several executors or administrators`

source.quote: Where probate or letters of administration have been granted to more than one executor or administrator, and one of them dies, the representation of the estate shall accrue to the surviving executor or executors or, except in cases to which section 6 applies, administrator or administrators.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 25(1)

readings.description: 'cases to which section 6 applies' means the s 6(2) CASES -- a minority or a life interest -- where the Act requires either a trust corporation or two individuals, so accrual to a single surviving administrator is exactly the outcome s 6(2) forbids.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 6(2) -- the requirement of a trust corporation or not less than 2 individuals, which accrual to one survivor would defeat

readings.description: Any case GOVERNED BY s 6, which is every grant, so administrators never take by accrual at all.
readings.rejection_rationale: It makes the words 'administrator or administrators' in the same sentence inoperative. An exception that swallows the class it qualifies is not a reading a court would reach.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 6(5) -- 'This section shall apply to grants made after 1 January 1935', which is what makes s 6 apply to every grant and so gives R2 its footing

taken.rationale: The verdict enum has four members and the s 6 case has its own: `the representation does not accrue, this being a case to which section 6 applies`. NOTE THE ASYMMETRY THE SUBSECTION DRAWS: the exception is attached to administrators only. Executors take by accrual in every case, because their title comes from the will and not from the grant.

witnesses: `letters to two administrators, one having died` over `the Tan intestacy`
`letters to two administrators, one having died` over the Ong estate with no will

site.anchor: `s 13(1) — letters of administration with the will annexed may be granted on failure of executors`

source.quote: Where — (a) no executor is appointed by a will; (b) the executor or all the executors appointed by will are legally incapable of acting as such, or have renounced the right to act as such; (c) no executor survives the testator; (d) all the executors die before obtaining probate or before having administered all the estate of the deceased; or (e) the executors appointed by any will do not appear and extract probate, letters of administration with the will annexed may be granted to such person or persons as the court considers the fittest to administer the estate.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 13(1)

readings.description: Where the will appoints NO executor, all five limbs are satisfied: `all` over an empty list is TRUE and limbs (c) and (e) are negatives over the same empty list, so on the bare words every limb answers yes.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 13(1)(a) -- 'no executor is appointed by a will', the limb that is satisfied in exactly that case and makes the disjunction true whatever the others do

readings.description: Limbs (b) to (e) PRESUPPOSE an executor -- 'the executor or all the executors appointed by will', 'no executor survives', 'all the executors die', 'the executors ... do not appear' -- and are neither true nor false where none was appointed.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 13(1)(b)-(e) -- each limb is stated of 'the executor(s) appointed by will', a definite description

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted; the presupposition reading is natural. It is non-operative because writing a non-emptiness condition into (b) to (e) would add words the section does not have to buy nothing -- the GATE gives the same answer either way, limb (a) being satisfied in exactly that case.

taken.rationale: The literal reading. Marked at the site rather than left to be discovered from a fixture, because a reader inspecting a SINGLE limb should know that (b) to (e) are vacuously satisfied on a will appointing nobody, even though the disjunction they feed is not affected.

notes: The readings differ per-limb and agree on the gate, which is why `extensionally-equivalent` and not `observable`: `the will appointing no executor` exercises the case but does not separate the readings at the only output the module reports.

site.anchor: `s 30 — letters of administration are granted to a creditor`

source.quote: When letters of administration are granted to a creditor, he may be required to enter into a bond to pay the debts of the deceased rateably, without preferring his own debt.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 30

readings.description: BOTH KINDS of grant, s 30 using 'letters of administration' as the genus, the way s 18(4)(c) does when it opens a grant 'to a creditor of the deceased'.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 13(2)(e) -- 'a creditor of the deceased' is expressly ranked for a grant of letters of administration WITH the will annexed

readings.description: Letters of administration SIMPLICITER ONLY, s 2 defining the two as separate terms.

citations.cite: Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 29(7) -- 'administrations whether with or without the will annexed'; and s 21(2), s 55(1)(c) -- all showing that the Act says both in as many words when it means both
