site.anchor: `the person is an infant on the date in question`
provisions: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 ss 3-21 ("infant", used throughout and defined nowhere)

source.quote: In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “court” means the General Division of the High Court or a Family Court.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 2 -- the whole of the interpretation section, which defines "court" and nothing else

readings.description: The general age of majority in Singapore, whatever it is, is imported into this Act: the drafter used an undefined word of art and meant the age the general law fixes.
readings.rejection_rationale: THE PREMISE FAILS ON THE FETCHED SOURCES. The Interpretation Act 1965 supplies no general age of majority -- source/IA1965.txt contains neither "age of majority" nor a definition of "minor" -- and Civil Law Act 1909 s 35 is confined to contractual capacity, with s 35(3)(b) expressly preserving the age requirements of other written laws rather than supplying one. There is no general age to import.

citations.cite: Interpretation Act 1965 (2020 Rev Ed) -- searched for "age of majority", "minor" and "majority"; no general age of majority is defined

Civil Law Act 1909 (2020 Rev Ed) s 35(1) -- 'as from 1 March 2009, a contract entered into by a minor who has attained the age of 18 years shall have effect as if he were of full age', a rule about contracts only

readings.description: 21, on the analogy of Wills Act 1838 s 4's "under 21 years of age", and on the strength of the three institutional layers that state the number: the probate rules, an obiter judicial statement, and the Family Justice Courts' own public guidance.

citations.cite: Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024 (S 723/2024) P.6 r 24(1) -- 'administration for his or her use and benefit until he or she attains 21 years of age'
TGT v TGU [2015] SGHCF 10 at [4] and [64]-[65] (Foo Tuat Yien JC) -- an infant is 'a child, who is less than 21 years old'; obiter, citing no statute
Wills Act 1838 (2020 Rev Ed) s 4 -- 'No will made by any person under 21 years of age shall be valid.' (quoted from source/WA1838.txt, not from this Act)

readings.foreclosure: NOTHING REFUTES 21 -- it is very probably the right number, and three institutional layers say so. What forecloses it here is that NONE OF THEM IS THIS ACT: r 24 states 21 for the duration of a grant under the Probate and Administration Act, TGT v TGU is a parenthesis in the closing observation of a forum non conveniens judgment citing nothing, and the Family Justice Courts' guidance page cites nothing whatever for the figure. Civil Law Act 1909 s 35(3)(b) preserves 'the application of any provision in any other written law stipulating a requirement as to the attainment of a particular age for the purposes of that written law' -- which keeps Wills Act s 4's twenty-one alive for the Wills Act and does not reach this one. Writing 21 into the Guardianship of Infants Act would be the right number reached by a route s 35(3)(b) forecloses.

readings.description: The Act fixes no age and the age comes from OUTSIDE it, as an input supplied with the facts. The module carries it as a parameter and never as a constant.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 2 -- the interpretation section defines "court" and nothing else; "infant" is used in every operative section and defined in none
Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 11(b) -- 'where the infant is of an age to express an independent opinion', the ONE age the Act names, which is a capacity left at large and not a majority

Civil Law Act 1909 (2020 Rev Ed) s 35(3)(b) -- Subsection (1) shall not affect or alter 'the application of any provision in any other written law stipulating a requirement as to the attainment of a particular age for the purposes of that written law.'

taken.rationale:
THE ENCODING NEVER WRITES A NUMBER, AND THE MATERIALISATION FOLLOWS FROM THAT RATHER THAN FROM A PREFERENCE. Two routes, both taking the age from outside. The first, `the person is an infant on the date in question`, reads `Person`'s already-construed `the date on which the person attains the age of majority` and compares it with the date in question, propagating NOTHING where the date is absent. The second, `the date on which the person attains the age of majority, computed from the date of birth`, takes `the age of majority, in years` as a plain GIVEN NUMBER, so a reader can see exactly where the number enters and that this Act did not supply it; the year is incremented rather than days added, which is leap-safe.

IT IS NOT AN `interpretation-field`, and the difference is not cosmetic. R4's shape is a field of an `Interpretation` record threaded as an ordinary GIVEN, with the readings as that field's enum constructors; there is no `Interpretation` record anywhere in this cleanroom, and the age is not an enum over R1 and R2 but an open NUMBER. So the fork is DELEGATED: the encoding reads a supplied fact and whoever supplies it decides, which is what `delegated-to-fact` names, and `fact-supplied` is the only mechanism honest to it.

CONTRAST THE WILLS ACT, WHICH DOES NOT DELEGATE. wills-act.l4 computes its own twenty-first anniversary from `date of birth` and is forbidden by family-domain.l4 to read the shared majority field at all, because s 4 stipulates 21 IN ITS OWN WORDS -- 'No will made by any person under 21 years of age shall be valid.' That is exactly the case Civil Law Act s 35(3)(b) preserves: a provision in a written law stipulating an age for the purposes of that written law. The Guardianship of Infants Act stipulates none, so nothing is preserved for it and nothing may be borrowed into it.

Status `open` rather than `resolved`: the module's own register says 'TAKEN: neither', and the schema requires a `taken` even so. What `taken` records here is the delegation, not a choice between R1 and R2.

witnesses: `the date on which the person attains the age of majority, computed from the date of birth` `Wei Ming, the infant` 21 = 19 July 2033, against the same decision at 18 = 19 July 2030 (§§§ `The age of majority is an input, not a fact of this Act`)
notes: THE SEARCH IS A CLAIM A READER CAN RUN, and the module states it exactly for that reason. source/GIA1934.txt returns nothing for `years of age`, `majority`, `minor`, `attain`, `21 years` or `18 years`; the only quantified durations in the Act are s 5A(3)(e)'s '12 months', s 16(1)(b)'s 'one year' and the 'per month' of s 18(1)'s cap. An earlier draft of the module's own entry also listed `age of` among the strings that return nothing, and that was wrong -- 'mortgage of' in s 18(2) contains it. Neither correction touches the conclusion.

E4 records that the Public Trustee's published practice releases Estate Monies at 21 and Nominated CPF Monies at 18, and says in one sentence 'when they reach the age of majority (either 18 or 21)'. It is cross-referenced as evidence that the number is not uniform even in practice; 18 is not offered here as a third reading of this Act, because nothing connects the CPF nomination rule to guardianship.
The evidential half of this silence -- what to do when the majority date is not recorded at all -- is a separate fork and is F-GIA-17.

site.anchor: `the court may appoint a guardian to act jointly with the mother under section 6(1)`

source.quote: When no guardian has been appointed by the father or if the guardian or guardians appointed by the father is or are dead or refuses or refuse to act, the court may if it thinks fit appoint a guardian to act jointly with the mother.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(1)

readings.description: ALL of the appointees are dead or refusing. The court's power arises only where every guardian the father appointed has dropped out.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(1) -- first sentence, 'either alone or jointly with any guardian appointed by the father', of which the second sentence is the exact complement on this reading

readings.description: ANY ONE of them is dead or refusing, so the court may step in as soon as one appointee drops out even if others are still acting.
readings.rejection_rationale: The court could then appoint a fourth guardian alongside two who are still acting, which the words 'to act jointly with the mother' do not obviously contemplate. R1 makes the second sentence the exact complement of the first, so the court's power arises precisely where the mother would otherwise be guardian alone.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(1) -- 'the guardian or guardians appointed by the father is or are dead or refuses or refuse to act', whose singular/plural pairing is what leaves the quantifier open

taken.rationale: `all` over the appointees. A CONSEQUENCE OF R1 WORTH KNOWING, and noted in place under s 6(1): it makes the first limb of the second sentence redundant, `all` over an empty list being TRUE, so 'When no guardian has been appointed by the father' is already covered by the second limb as encoded.

witnesses: `Wei Ming, the father having appointed two guardians, one of them dead`
notes: THE MODULE MEASURED THE DISCRIMINATION RATHER THAN ASSERTING IT: the named file is the ONLY one that separates the readings -- everywhere else a parent has at most one appointee, where ALL and ANY coincide -- and changing `all` to `any` in the rule turns exactly one assertion red.

site.anchor: `the guardians appointed by the father who are able and willing to act`

source.quote: On the death of the father of an infant, the mother, if surviving, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be guardian of the infant, either alone or jointly with any guardian appointed by the father.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(1)

readings.description: LITERALLY EVERY APPOINTEE counts as a guardian appointed by the father, including one who is dead or refuses to act, because the phrase records a historical fact of appointment.
readings.rejection_rationale: A dead guardian cannot act jointly with anybody, and the second sentence of s 6(1) exists to fill exactly that hole -- so on this reading the two sentences would overlap rather than complement each other.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(1) -- 'any guardian appointed by the father', which on its face describes an appointment and not a capacity

readings.description: Only those ABLE AND WILLING TO ACT count, because what the provision does with the appointment is make the appointee act jointly.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(1) -- the second sentence treats an appointee who 'is or are dead or refuses or refuse to act' as absent for the purpose of deciding whether the court should supply somebody
Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 7(5) -- 'Where guardians are appointed by both parents, the guardians so appointed shall after the death of the surviving parent act jointly.'

taken.rationale: `the guardians appointed by the father who are able and willing to act` filters the appointees, and the same filter is now applied at s 7(5). It was NOT applied there before: an earlier draft counted the APPOINTMENTS in s 7(5)'s gate and the APPOINTEES in its answer, and so reported joint action by one man.

witnesses: `Wei Ming, the testamentary guardian refusing to act`
`Wei Ming, both parents dead and the father's only appointee dead`
notes: A THIRD PLACE, WHERE THE READING IS MORE OF A STRETCH AND THE MODULE SAYS SO. `the guardians appointed by the father` also drops a guardian the court has REMOVED under s 10, and that list feeds the second sentence's first limb, 'When no guardian has been appointed by the father'. Read literally that limb is about the historical fact of an appointment, and a guardian appointed and then removed does not make it true that none was appointed. The reading taken is purposive -- after the removal the mother is guardian alone, which is the state the second sentence exists to relieve -- and little turns on it, because s 10 gives the court its own power to appoint another in his place. The two routes are different and a reader should know which one the module reports. Carried here rather than as an entry of its own, to keep the 1:1 map with the module's register.

E44 (UPD v UPC [2019] SGHCF 25) supports R2 from the bench, obiter and on a different subsection: s 8's trigger is persons who 'act as joint guardians', not persons formally appointed as such -- 'a predicate an encoding would naturally get backwards by keying on the appointment event rather than the factual role', which is precisely the error R1 would be. It does not settle s 6(1) and this entry does not claim it does.

E39 (VET v VEU [2020] SGHCF 4) bears on the s 10 stretch above and cuts against part of it: 'guardian' in s 10 does not include a parent, so the removal power cannot be used against a natural parent at all, despite ss 6(1)-(2) denominating a surviving parent 'guardian of the infant'. The module carries `the parent has been removed from his guardianship by the court under section 10` and so models a removal this authority says cannot happen. Recorded here as a bearing on the encoding; it is not a reading of this fork and is not asserted as settling it.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7(3)

readings.rejection_rationale: s 7(4) says that if the court refuses to make any order 'the mother or father shall remain sole guardian', and 'remain' only makes sense if the parent was already sole -- which she cannot have been if the appointee was acting alongside or alone.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 7(3) -- the 'unless' limb removes the words 'act jointly' and says nothing about what replaces them

readings.description: He DOES NOT ACT AT ALL pending an order of the court under s 7(4).

site.anchor: `the infant has no guardian of the person`

source.quote: Where an infant has no parent, no guardian of the person and no other person having parental rights with respect to him, the court, on the application of any person, may, if it thinks fit, appoint the applicant to be the guardian of the infant.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 6(3)

readings.description: The limb asks WHO HAS BEEN APPOINTED, so a guardian of the person who is dead, refuses to act, or has been removed still counts and the gate stays shut.
readings.rejection_rationale: An infant whose only guardian had died would then have no guardian and no route to one, which cannot be right. Death and removal need no argument -- a dead man is nobody's guardian, and s 10 ends the guardianship of the one it removes.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(3) -- 'no guardian of the person', a phrase capable of describing the appointment rather than the office as held

readings.description: The limb asks WHO IS THERE, so none of the three counts and the gate opens.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(1) -- an appointee who 'is or are dead or refuses or refuse to act' is treated as absent for the purpose of deciding whether the court should step in, and s 6(3) is a gate of the same character
Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 10 -- the removal power, which ends the guardianship of the person removed

taken.rationale: `the infant has no guardian of the person` reads the limb through `the standing of the guardian under this Act`, so a testamentary appointee whose appointing parent is still alive, and one the surviving parent has objected to under s 7(3), are not counted either -- neither case can arise inside s 6(3)'s own gate, and the reason for doing it anyway is that it makes this answer and `the persons who are guardians of the infant` two readings of one predicate over the guardian RECORDS. THAT WAS ONCE STATED AS 'AND SO INCAPABLE OF CONTRADICTING EACH OTHER', AND IT WAS NOT TRUE, because the records are not the only guardians: s 6 makes the surviving parent guardian by force of the section and without any record, so a count reading records only could not see her. On the plainest facts in the file -- the father dead, the mother alive, nobody appointed -- the module said the guardians of this infant were the mother AND that the infant had no guardian of his person. The limb now has a second conjunct that reads the s 6 parent.

witnesses: `Wei Ming, an orphan whose only guardian of the person has died`
`Wei Ming, an orphan whose only guardian of the person refuses to act`
notes: A SEPARATE READING RIDES ON THAT SECOND CONJUNCT and should be seen for what it is: that a parent who is 'guardian of the infant' under s 6 is a guardian of his PERSON. ss 6(1)-(2) make the survivor guardian of the infant simpliciter and do not divide the office into person and property, while s 6(3) asks after a guardian 'of the person'. Reading the undivided office as including the person is the only reading that makes s 6(3) work: on the other, an infant with a living mother would have no guardian of his person and the court could appoint a stranger over her head. Carried here rather than as an entry of its own.

E38 (VET v VEU [2020] SGHCF 4) is cross-referenced because it construes the appointment powers this gate belongs to -- s 5 is NOT a power to appoint a guardian, and s 6, sub-section (3) included, is. It confirms the gate is an appointment power; it does not decide what 'no guardian of the person' counts.

site.anchor: `the guardian has done a thing section 16(1) forbids`

source.quote: A guardian of the property of an infant shall not, without the permission of the court — (a) sell, mortgage, exchange, or otherwise part with the possession of any of the movable or immovable property of the infant; or

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 16(1)

readings.description: A lease of a year or less is STILL CAUGHT BY LIMB (a) -- a lease parts with possession -- so limb (b) merely spells out the long-lease case.
readings.rejection_rationale: The words 'for a term exceeding one year' would then do no work at all. A limb that adds nothing to the one above it is not a reading to prefer.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 16(1)(a) -- 'or otherwise part with the possession of any of the movable or immovable property of the infant', which on its face covers a lease of any length

readings.description: Limb (b) is the SPECIFIC PROVISION for leases and displaces limb (a) for them, so a lease of a year or less is outside s 16(1) altogether.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 16(1)(b) -- 'lease any land belonging to the infant for a term exceeding one year', a limb whose qualifying words presuppose that shorter leases are permitted

taken.rationale: The encoding LEAVES THE CHOICE VISIBLE rather than burying it: limb (a) is a recorded fact (`has sold, mortgaged, exchanged, or otherwise parted with the possession of any of the movable or immovable property of the infant`), so a case file that records a short lease as a parting with possession will make the prohibition bite; and limb (b) computes from a recorded term.

witnesses: `a guardian of the property who granted a one-year lease`
notes: A SIMPLIFICATION ON THE SAME (a)/(b) BOUNDARY, recorded with this entry rather than as one of its own. s 16(1) requires 'the permission of the court' for either limb and family-domain.l4 carries ONE permission flag for both, so a guardian permitted to grant a long lease under (b) reads as permitted to sell under (a). s 16(3) tells against that -- the court 'shall not make any order under subsection (1) unless it is necessary or advisable in the interests of the infant', and necessity is judged of the dealing proposed -- so the true shape is one permission per dealing. Splitting the flag means adding a field to family-domain.l4, which three other Act modules build against, so it is named rather than done. THE ERROR IS PERMISSIVE: a case file must not record the permission unless the court's permission in fact covered the dealing in question.

E8 is cross-referenced because the word the encoding quotes is an amended one: Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Act 2021 s 132 deleted 'leave' in ss 16(1) and 18(1) and substituted 'permission' with effect from 15 October 2024, which is in the fetched text. Terminological only.

`a GIA weekly provision of $24`

site.anchor: `the infant has a parent or parents`

source.quote: The court, in exercising the powers conferred by this Act, must have regard primarily to the welfare of the infant, and must consider — (a) where the infant has a parent or parents — the wishes of the parent or both of them, as the case may be; and (b) where the infant is of an age to express an independent opinion — the wishes of the infant.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 11

readings.description: A parent NOT IN EVIDENCE is not counted, so the limb is answered from the records as they stand and the list of matters is shorter by one.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 11(a) -- 'where the infant has a parent or parents', a condition to be made out on the material before the court

readings.description: The absence of a record is not evidence of the absence of a parent, so the limb should be treated as OPEN where no parent is recorded.
readings.rejection_rationale: It abandons the discipline family-domain.l4 states for s 6(3) -- a missing record never manufactures a fact, in either direction. Note the two provisions cut OPPOSITE ways on that one discipline, which is why it is stated as a discipline and not as a convenience: in s 6(3) it CLOSES a gate, and here it SHORTENS a list.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(3) -- 'Where an infant has no parent', the same fact asked for the opposite purpose

taken.rationale: `the infant has a parent or parents` answers from the recorded parents only.

witnesses: `Wei Ming, the mother dead and the father not in evidence`
notes: A SECOND, SEPARATE CHOICE IS TAKEN IN THE SAME LIMB and was not recorded before the module's later rounds: the parent must also be ALIVE. A dead parent's wishes can be evidenced -- in a will, for instance -- so it is not obvious that s 11(a) stops at the survivors. The reason for reading it that way is internal consistency: s 6(3)'s 'an infant has no parent' is answered by both parents being dead, so within one Act 'has a parent' would otherwise be used in two senses, and an orphan would have a parent for s 11(a) and none for s 6(3). Carried here rather than as an entry of its own.

E5 AND E6 ARE THE REASON THIS SITE NEEDS READING WITH A DATE IN HAND. s 11 was WHOLLY REPLACED with effect from 31 January 2024 by Family Justice Reform Act 2023 s 14 -- the quoted text is the replacement, and paragraph (b) is new -- while FJRA s 45(7) preserves the OLD s 11 for any proceedings commenced BEFORE that date. Two texts of s 11 are simultaneously in force, selected by the date proceedings began, and the savings rule appears nowhere in the GIA. This corpus carries no rule-version axis, so the module encodes the replacement as a single rule and will answer pre-31/01/2024 proceedings with a limb the law did not then contain. That is a currency gap and not a fork, and it is recorded here because this is the entry a reader of s 11 will reach.

site.anchor: `the parent who survived the other`

source.quote: If a guardian has been appointed by the court to act jointly with a surviving parent, he shall continue to act as guardian after the death of the surviving parent; but if the surviving parent has appointed a guardian, the guardian appointed by the court shall act jointly with the guardian appointed by the surviving parent.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 7(6)

readings.description: FALL BACK ON A DEFAULT where the comparison of dates of death fails -- one date unknown, or both parents dying on the same day.
readings.rejection_rationale: The alternative would be to invent a fact. Which parent survived the other is a question of fact the record does not answer, and a default answer would be indistinguishable from a found one.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 7(6) -- 'a surviving parent', which presupposes that one of them is identifiable as the survivor

readings.description: SAY THAT IT CANNOT BE DETERMINED, giving the standing type a member of its own for the case.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 7(6) -- the subsection turns on the identity of the surviving parent for its second half, and the Act supplies no commorientes rule

taken.rationale: `The standing of a guardian under this Act` carries a member for exactly this case. BUT WHAT CANNOT BE DETERMINED IS ONLY HALF THE SUBSECTION, and an earlier draft said it was the whole. s 7(6) asks two questions: whether the court's appointee 'shall continue to act as guardian after the death of the surviving parent', and whom he then acts jointly with. The first needs only that the surviving parent be DEAD, and where BOTH parents are dead that is so whichever of them survived; only the second needs the survivor identified. So the standing type now has a member saying he continues to act and that whom he acts jointly with is open, and the old member is kept for the case where a parent is NOT IN EVIDENCE -- there, a living parent who objected under s 7(3) would stop him acting at all, so whether he acts really is open.

`Wei Ming, both parents dead but one death undated`

source.quote: Unless the court otherwise orders, nothing in this Act shall apply to any money paid into a District Court to the credit of an infant in any action or proceeding in a District Court or to any money in a District Court ordered to be transferred to the credit of an infant, but the same shall be dealt with according to the Rules of Court.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 21

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 2 -- 'In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “court” means the General Division of the High Court or a Family Court.'

readings.description: It is the DISTRICT COURT holding the money, the section being about that court's own funds and its own Rules.
readings.rejection_rationale: s 2 governs 'In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires', and s 21 gives no reason to depart -- the section names the District Court expressly three times and 'the court' once, which is a contrast rather than a synonym.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 21 -- 'money paid into a District Court', named as such, beside the unqualified 'the court'

taken.rationale: THE ENCODING DOES NOT TURN ON IT, and that is stated rather than left to be discovered: the fact recorded is that an order was made, not which forum made it, so `whether this Act applies to the money` gives the same answer on either reading.

source.quote: A guardian of the property of an infant may make reasonable provision out of the income of such property for his maintenance and education, having regard to his station in life; but no sum exceeding $100 per month may be so applied without the permission of the court.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 18(1)
Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 18(2) -- 'the court may order that provision for such purpose be made out of the capital of the infant’s property'

readings.description: HE MAY NOT, by expressio unius: s 18(1) empowers him 'out of the income of such property' and s 18(2) puts capital in the hands of the court, so the two subsections between them exhaust the routes.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 18(1) -- 'out of the income of such property', the guardian's own power expressly confined

Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 16(1) -- the guardian may not without the permission of the court 'sell, mortgage, exchange, or otherwise part with the possession of any of the movable or immovable property of the infant', which is how capital would have to be realised

readings.description: s 18(2) merely ADDS A COURT ROUTE without withdrawing anything, leaving s 16(1)'s permission requirement to do all the work -- on which reading a guardian WITH the court's permission to sell could apply the proceeds himself.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 18(2) -- the subsection confers a power on the court and says nothing about withdrawing one from the guardian
Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 16(1) -- read as the sole gate on dealings with capital, permission under it would carry the application of the proceeds with it

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted: the Act nowhere says the guardian may not resort to capital, and R2 needs no words added to any subsection. Non-operative because the module states the negative as a constant.

taken.rationale: `the guardian may of his own motion make provision out of the capital of the infant's property` MEANS FALSE. IT IS THE ONLY INFERENCE IN THIS MODULE STATED AS A BARE CONSTANT THAT THE ACT DOES NOT STATE IN TERMS -- the other constant, s 5A(5)(b)'s, is the subsection's own parenthesis -- which is why it is in the register at all. Whatever permission the guardian holds under s 18(1) is about the SIZE of a payment out of income, not about its source.

site.anchor: `section 3 reaches proceedings before the forum`

source.quote: Where in any proceedings before any court the custody or upbringing of an infant or the administration of any property belonging to or held in trust for an infant or the application of the income thereof is in question, the court, in deciding that question, shall regard the welfare of the infant as the first and paramount consideration

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 3

readings.description: s 2 GOVERNS, so s 3 binds only the General Division of the High Court and a Family Court.
readings.rejection_rationale: On this reading a District Court could decide an infant's custody without regarding his welfare as paramount, which the section plainly does not intend. Every other operative section says 'the court'; s 3 is the one that says 'any court'.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 2 -- 'In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “court” means the General Division of the High Court or a Family Court.'

readings.description: 'any court' is a CONTEXT THAT OTHERWISE REQUIRES within s 2's own proviso, so s 3 binds every forum.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 3 -- 'Where in any proceedings before any court', the only place in the Act where the wider phrase is used
Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 2 -- 'unless the context otherwise requires', the proviso this reading turns on

taken.rationale: `section 3 reaches proceedings before the forum` is the one place in the module where the wider `Forum` type does operative work; s 5A(7) and s 21, the other two places the Act names a forum outside s 2, are declined for other reasons. NOTE WHAT 'OPERATIVE' DOES AND DOES NOT MEAN HERE: the reading is written into the code and asserted over every member, but because s 3 reaches every forum the ANSWER is the same for all three -- which is exactly the point of R2, and is why the conjunct discriminates nothing.

notes: E43 (XLK v XLJ [2025] SGHC(A) 22) is cross-referenced because it is the most recent statement of s 3's reach: considerations of comity do not override the welfare principle, and s 3 continues to apply in all child-related custody disputes not brought under the International Child Abduction Act. It supports the breadth R2 gives the section; it does not decide the forum question, which is what this fork is.

provisions: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 ss 3-21 ("infant", used throughout and defined nowhere)

source.quote: In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “court” means the General Division of the High Court or a Family Court.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) s 2 -- the Act's whole interpretation section, which supplies no age and no evidential provision

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted -- probate-administration-act.l4 takes exactly this reading (F-PAA-A2) and is right to on its own Act. It is non-operative here because THIS Act supplies no age at all (F-GIA-01), so there is no test to fail: folding to FALSE would report 'not an infant' on the strength of a number this Act does not contain.

readings.description: FOLD IT TO 'AN INFANT', since the Act's provisions are protective and the cost of a wrong answer is asymmetric.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 6(3) and s 16(1) -- provisions that exist to supply an infant with a guardian and to restrain that guardian, whose failure mode is one-sided

readings.foreclosure: Not refuted; it is the safer default for a protective statute. Non-operative for the same reason as R1 -- there is no test here to pass either -- and because it would put a positive finding of infancy on a record that contains none.

readings.description: REFUSE BOTH FOLDS and report that the question cannot be determined, giving the verdict a member of its own so that a consumer cannot mistake it for either fold.

citations.cite: Guardianship of Infants Act 1934 s 2 -- the Act defines only "court", so it fixes no age and contains no evidential provision answering to Probate and Administration Act 1934 s 6(3), and names no forum to which the silence could be routed

taken.rationale:
`the person is an infant on the date in question` returns a MAYBE BOOLEAN and propagates NOTHING, and `Whether this Act has an infant to govern` gives that case a named member -- `whether the person is an infant on that date cannot be determined, the date on which he attains the age of majority not being in evidence`. A consumer that needs a boolean must choose its own fold, and this module refuses to choose one for it.

THIS IS THE ONE PLACE THE FOUR MODULES GIVE ONE QUESTION THREE SHAPES, and none of them said so before the cross-module round. probate-administration-act.l4 folds to FALSE (F-PAA-A2), justified by its own s 6(3), which routes the evidential question to a forum; wills-act.l4 carries a distinct verdict for it (F-WA-A1) and computes from `date of birth` because Wills Act s 4 states a number; intestate-succession-act.l4 never asks. All three are defensible and all three are now cross-referenced at their sites.

WHAT IS NOT IN DISPUTE: wherever this module and the Probate and Administration Act module both give an answer they give the SAME one, boundary included, because both read the shared `the date on which the person attains the age of majority` and both compare it strictly. They part only in the silent case.

witnesses: `Wei Ming, majority date not in evidence, the father having died leaving a testamentary guardian`
